18b4eaa51b.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′24.49″.
18b4eaa51b.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′24.49″, 0°37′06.93″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′43.42″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′36.81″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′07.91″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°37′54.29″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

18e1af24a9.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Gananathar, a devout Brahmana from Sirkali, was the 38th of the Nayanmars. He was revered for his deep devotion to Bhagavan Shiva and was a source of spiritual guidance for many. Recognizing the varied abilities of those who sought his advice, he engaged them in service activities related to the temple, such as cleaning, making garlands, gardening, and lamp lighting. This approach not only transformed these individuals into Shiva Bhaktas but also infused a sense of devotion in them. Additionally, Gananathar was deeply devoted to Jnana Sambandar. All these great attributes contributed to him earning the grace of Bhagavan Shiva.
18e1af24a9.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

192e59ed48.d:
When the transit of the Sun (saṅkrānti) happens in the second half of the day (aparāhṇa) and before midnight, the second half of the day form a puṇyakāla for various observances. In addition to 16 ghatikas on either side of the transition, and specific puṇyakālas like ṣaḍaśīti, viṣṇupadī etc., this is also useful, especially in cases where the other puṇyakālas are inconvenient for appropriate performance of rituals such as snāna, dāna, tarpaṇa, etc.

While the nirayana puṇyakāla-s are well known, marked by the transit of the Sun into various rāśī-s (which confer the name to the corresponding saura month), there are also ayana-s and sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s, which mark the position of the Sun above the Northern or Southern parts of the Earth. These determine the r̥tu-s, and also the very famous uttarāyaṇa and dakṣināyana (movement of the Sun towards North or South, respectively). While these two types of puṇyakāla-s (sāyana and nirayana) coincided millennia ago, there has been a gradual precession of the equinoxes, owing to the nature of the Earth's rotation, causing the sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s to happen about 24 days before the nirayana saṅkramaṇa-s. In that era, uttarāyaṇa coincided with makara-saṅkramaṇa and dakṣināyana coincided with karkaṭaka-saṅkramaṇa, and the mēsa and tulā saṅkramaṇa-s corresponded to the equinoxes, when the Sun rises direct East (and sets direct West).

Many Dharma Shastra texts recognise the separate puṇyakāla-s for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. The vachanam of Jaabaali Maharshi is mentioned above, where he says that the puṇyakāla-s are identical (in their reckoning) for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. In the Pulastya Siddhanta, the anushthanas which are to be performed in this sayana punya kala just like nirayana are explicitly stated: snāna, dāna, japa, śrāddha, vrata, hōma, etc. In Kala Madhava, which is considered as the source text of the kala vicharas of the Dikshitiya, it is said in the 5th prakarana that,  meṣādi-saṅkrāntayo yasmin dine bhavanti tasmād dināt pūrvebhyaḥ ekādaśabhyo dinebhyaḥ prācīne dine, noting that Sayana Sankramanas occurred ~11 days before the day when the Mesha Sankramanas etc occur. Further references are seen in Dharma Sindhu first pariccheda, Jayasimha Kalpadruma sankranti nirnaya and Nirnaya Sindhu first pariccheda. There are also ample references in Vedas, illustrating how Ayana-s happened much later (in certain other eras), e.g. Shukla Yajur Veda Shatapatha Brahmana (Ekapaat Kanda 1/2/3), Nakshatra Sukta belonging to the Atharva Veda (Shaunaka Samhita 19/7/2), Maitrayaniya Aranyaka (6/14), and Taittiriya Brahmana (1/5/2).

For a wonderfully detailed exposition on the topic, see https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/dakshinayana-en and https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/uttarayana-en .

𑌜𑌾𑌬𑌾𑌲𑌿𑌃---  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍀𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾।

194bb1e3eb.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śukraḥ in śravaṇaḥ makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°41′09.66″.
194bb1e3eb.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°41′09.66″, 0°41′02.30″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at śravaṇaḥ-4 makaraḥ (latitude 2°00′24.91″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.28, elongation 5°47′39.39″ E). śukraḥ at śravaṇaḥ-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°19′15.25″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 5°35′40.25″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1986cd6c9d.d:
The Phalguna Paurnami festival is a grand five-day celebration held annually at the Swami Pushkarini. Each day of the festival features a different set of deities taken for a celestial ride on a beautifully decorated float in the temple tank.

1. On the first day, Bhagavan Rama, along with Sita and Lakshmana, are worshipped and taken for a ride on the float.
2. The second day is dedicated to Bhagavan Krishna and Rukmini, who are also offered puja and taken on the float for a pleasure ride.

For the last three days, from Trayodashi to Paurnami:
1. Sri Malayappa Swami, accompanied by Sridevi and Bhudevi, are taken out for a ride in the temple tank.
2. The third day includes three rounds of the float, increasing to five rounds on the next day.
3. On the final day, the utsava murtis (festival deities) are taken for a splendid ride on the float for seven rounds, attracting a large number of pilgrims. The beauty of the deities is further enhanced by the charm of the full moon, making this day particularly special and visually stunning.

19b2b342b2.b: Observed on Pūrvāṣāḍhā nakshatra of Dhanuḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
19b2b342b2.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

This Nayanmar, a Vellala from Tirucchangamangai, grew disillusioned with worldly life and yearned for liberation. Initially swayed by Buddhist teachings, he eventually found his spiritual calling in Shaivism, convinced that intense devotion to Bhagavan Shiva was the true path to liberation. Despite maintaining the outward appearance of a Buddhist, his heart was devoted to Bhagavan Shiva.

In an unusual display of devotion, he would sit in an open Shiva temple, deeply meditating on the Lingam. One day, in a state of divine absorption, he unwittingly threw a stone at the Lingam. Realizing this act the next day, he interpreted it as divine will, understanding that Bhagavan Shiva accepts any offering made with sincere devotion. Henceforth, throwing a stone at the Lingam became his unique form of daily worship, a ritual he performed before eating.

On one occasion, just as he was about to eat, he remembered he had not performed his daily ritual. Driven by devotion, he rushed to the temple to throw a stone at the Lingam! Touched by his unorthodox yet profound devotion, Bhagavan Shiva appeared before him, blessed him, and ultimately took him to Kailasa, the abode of the divine.
19b2b342b2.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

19faf6d7ff.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in mūlā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°18′38.97″.
19faf6d7ff.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°18′38.97″, 0°18′31.14″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°00′05.75″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.28, elongation 26°56′24.90″ E). śukraḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°18′44.72″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 26°57′09.26″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1a022d3efb.b: Event occured on 1733-01-20 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
1a022d3efb.d:
On this day (date merits verification), hakIkat rAi (Haqiqat Rai Bakhmal Puri), about 15 years old, was beheaded by the then punjAbI muslim government of Zakariya Khan. Quasi Abdul Haq, who was responsible for the Fatwa, was also beheaded later on by Sardar Dal Singh and Saradar Mana Singh and shown around the city of Batala.

Background: One day, some of his Muslim classmates ridiculed Hindu goddess Devi Ma. He ultimately responded by ridiculing Fatima, daughter of Prophet Muhammad. The Muslim boys complained to the maulvis. Haqiqat Rai was arrested and sent to Amir Beg, the administrator of Sialkot. Amir said Haqiqat Rai had committed a sin and he can be pardoned only if he accepts Islam as punishment for blasphemy. Haqiqat Rai refused conversion to Islam. Haqiqat Rai's parents tried to change his mind, but failed. He was then sent to Zakaria Khan, the Governor of Lahore. But Haqiqat Rai did not agree to convert even under further torture. Then he was killed.

Before execution, Hakikat Rai Puri was allowed to take a sacred bath, perform a Gau Daan and listen Gita from a Pandit. He is depicted with a shikhA and a tilak.

The day of his execution used to be marked by a 'mela' (fair) on Vasant Panchami day in Lahore, around his 'samadhi' (Baway di marrhi), before India's partition.

1a29227417.d:
The Krishna-paksha Ekadashi of jyaiṣṭha month is known as yōginī-ēkādaśī.

The fruits of fasting on Ekādaśī are greatly extolled in the Padma Purana—

A person who bathes at Śaṃkhoddhāra and beholds the image of Viṣṇu does not acquire even a sixteenth of the merit earned by fasting on Ekādaśī. O noble king, even if one gives four lakhs of coins on the days of the Sun's transition between Zodiac signs, it does not equal even a sixteenth of the merit from an Ekādaśī fast! Indeed, fasting on Ekādaśī grants the same religious merit as bathing at Prabhāsa during a lunar or solar eclipse. One who drinks the sacred water at Kedāra is freed from rebirth, and likewise, fasting on Ekādaśī removes the cycle of rebirth.

The merit from an Ekādaśī fast is a hundred times greater than the reward of performing an Ashvamedha sacrifice on earth. Fasting on Ekādaśī yields a hundredfold more merit than gifting a thousand cows to a learned brāhmaṇa. Those who fast on Ekādaśī are considered equal to those whose bodies are inhabited by Brahma, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The merit from observing the Ekādaśī vow is immeasurable, and difficult to obtain even by the Devas. There is no other vow like that of the Ekādaśī, that destroys sins.
1a29227417.s:
𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍋𑌷𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌯𑌦𑍀𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌃।  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨 𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍁𑌭𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌿॥  
  
𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌰𑌮𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰।  
𑌭𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌰𑍀𑌕𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷 𑌶𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌮𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌦𑌥𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍇 𑌕𑍇𑌶𑌵 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵।  
𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚 𑌵𑍈 𑌵𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑍋 𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌤𑌃॥  
--𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇  
  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌸𑍌𑌤𑌿𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑌿𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌦𑍇𑌶𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌿𑌂𑌶𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃---  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌂 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍀 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇।  
𑌸 𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍈𑌕𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍈 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋 𑌵𑌯𑌃॥௧௪॥  
  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍋𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌂 𑌗𑌦𑌾𑌧𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௩௫॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌨𑍃𑌪𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮॥௩௬॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍।

𑌤𑌪𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍋 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍇 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌤𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌃॥௪௦॥

𑌗𑍋𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌗𑍇॥௪௧॥

𑌯𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌃॥௪௨॥  
𑌵𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍁𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍋 𑌯𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌕𑌾𑌃॥௪௩॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇।  
𑌏𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍁𑌰𑍈𑌰𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌭𑌮𑍍॥௪௪॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌸𑌮𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௧௧௮॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌶𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌉𑌮𑌾𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿-𑌮𑍁𑌰𑌵𑌧𑍋 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌚𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌂𑌶𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃॥௪௦॥

1a38f52301.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°29′38.36″.
1a38f52301.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°29′38.36″, 0°29′18.48″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′56.03″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 3°59′30.85″ E). śukraḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°24′34.39″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 4°07′59.83″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1a3d2e6cb3.b: Partial solar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈1.6 of 12 aṅgulas), Sun at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
1a3d2e6cb3.d: Magnitude: 14% of the solar diameter is covered (parimāṇa ≈1.6 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 03:07►16:56 (from 4 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra punarvasuḥ/puṣyaḥ/āśrēṣā (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or anūrādhā (anujanma) or uttaraprōṣṭhapadā (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: karkaṭaḥ, siṁhaḥ, dhanuḥ, mēṣaḥ get more ashubha phala, vr̥śchikaḥ, makaraḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam somewhat ashubha, kanyā, tulā, kumbhaḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

1a5784e7bd.d:
The Shukla-paksha Ekadashi of pauṣa month is known as pauṣa-putradā-ēkādaśī.

The fruits of fasting on Ekādaśī are greatly extolled in the Padma Purana—

A person who bathes at Śaṃkhoddhāra and beholds the image of Viṣṇu does not acquire even a sixteenth of the merit earned by fasting on Ekādaśī. O noble king, even if one gives four lakhs of coins on the days of the Sun's transition between Zodiac signs, it does not equal even a sixteenth of the merit from an Ekādaśī fast! Indeed, fasting on Ekādaśī grants the same religious merit as bathing at Prabhāsa during a lunar or solar eclipse. One who drinks the sacred water at Kedāra is freed from rebirth, and likewise, fasting on Ekādaśī removes the cycle of rebirth.

The merit from an Ekādaśī fast is a hundred times greater than the reward of performing an Ashvamedha sacrifice on earth. Fasting on Ekādaśī yields a hundredfold more merit than gifting a thousand cows to a learned brāhmaṇa. Those who fast on Ekādaśī are considered equal to those whose bodies are inhabited by Brahma, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The merit from observing the Ekādaśī vow is immeasurable, and difficult to obtain even by the Devas. There is no other vow like that of the Ekādaśī, that destroys sins.

1a6b681858.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in mūlā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°18′37.71″.
1a6b681858.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°18′37.71″, 0°18′29.88″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°00′03.54″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.28, elongation 26°56′19.18″ E). śukraḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°18′41.25″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 26°57′03.52″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1a78224d62.d: When the Ekadashi tithi is incident at sunrise on two consecutive days, the second day, where there is association with Dvadashi tithi, is known as unmīlanī is one of the eight mahādvādaśīs. The day on which Ekādaśī continues through day and night and extends for a ghaṭikā into the next day is known as Unmīlanī, and it is especially beloved by Bhagavan Viṣṇu. The combined sanctity of all holy and sacred places in the three worlds pales in comparison to even a fraction of the merit of Unmīlanī, as do sacrifices and austerities. There has never been, nor will there ever be, anything like Unmīlanī! The moment one worships Bhagavan Viṣṇu on the Unmīlanī day, all their accumulated (heaps of) sins fall (away) instantly. O king, Bhagavan Viṣṇu should be worshipped with great effort, using the name of the month in which the Unmīlanī day occurs.

1a8118daa1.b: Observed on Śukla-Navamī tithi of Kārttikaḥ (lunar) month (Āśvinaḥ/paraviddha).

1a8e1b6bb9.d:
The celestial wedding of Bhagavan Srinivasa and Devi Padmavati is a grand festival held annually in the month of Vaishakha. The beautifully adorned Parinayotsavam Mandapam, set amidst the Narayanagiri gardens, serves as the enchanting venue for this three-day event, celebrated under the moonlit sky. The festivities unfold on the auspicious days of Navami, Dashami, and Ekadashi in the month of Vaishakha, featuring Sri Malayappaswami, Shri Venkateshwara's festival deity. Each day, he makes a grand entrance on different Vahanas: the Gaja (elephant), Ashva (horse), and Garuda (eagle), while Devi-s Sridevi and Bhudevi grace the event on separate palanquins.

Following the wedding rituals at the Parinayotsava Mandapam, a traditional 'Koluvu' gathering takes place, filled with the recitation of Vedic hymns and devotional songs. Bhagavan, accompanied by Sridevi and Bhudevi, then majestically returns to the temple.

Each day's festivities are marked by unique traditional rituals. On the first day, the arrival of Bhagavan Malayappa Swami on the celestial Gaja Vahanam, along with his consorts on their palanquins, is a sight to behold. The traditional wedding ceremony is conducted, where Bhagavan is seated in the ornately decorated Parinaya Mandapam, with his consorts positioned opposite him.

The ceremony includes several traditional rituals such as Edurukolu (mutual reception), Pula Bantata (game of flower balls), and Vastra Dharanam (offering of new clothes). These customs are observed over all three days. The grand finale of the divine marriage is marked by a spectacular display of fireworks, adding to the ceremony's splendor. The event concludes with a procession where Bhagavan Malayappa Swami, along with Devi-s Sridevi and Bhudevi, return to the main temple.

1aae5d3f95.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°29′38.09″.
1aae5d3f95.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°29′38.09″, 0°29′18.20″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′55.92″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 3°59′30.29″ E). śukraḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°24′34.01″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 4°07′59.26″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1ae6cd2af9.d: When a tripādanakṣatra is conjoined with a bhadrā tithi i.e. dvitīyā, saptamī or dvādaśī, and this falls on a Tuesday, Sunday or Saturday, it is known as a tripuṣkara-yōgaḥ. The dvipuṣkara occurs when the bhadrā tithis coincide with the same days as above, but with the dvipāda nakṣatras, which are mr̥gaśīrṣa, chitrā and dhaniṣṭhā. Like the tripuṣkara which gives a three-fold multiplier for śubha and aśubha, the dvipuṣkara has a two-fold effect.

1b1e8f684d.b: Event occured on 1526-11-15 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
1b1e8f684d.d:
On this day, Hemachandra vikramAditya, aka Hemu, was vanquished by mogols invading under akbar and his regent bairAm khAn (though they stayed in the rear - 8 miles away). This king, also known as Vikramaditya had won 22 battles against the Afghan rebels from 1553–1556 from Punjab to Bengal, and had his coronation at Purana Quila in Delhi on 7 October 1556 and had established ‘Hindu Raj’ in North India, before the 2nd battle of Panipat.

Events
Hemu was aided by afghAn-s who had been earlier deposed by bAbur's invasion. Hemu was atop an elephant named hawAi. His left was led by his sister's son, Ramya, and the right by Shadi Khan Kakkar.

Mogol army was led by Ali Quli Khan Shaibani in the center, Sikandar Khan Uzbak on the right and Abdulla Khan Uzbak towards the left. Vanguard led by Husain Quli Beg and Shah Quli Mahram.

Both the wings of the Mughal army had been driven back and Hemu moved his contingent of war elephants and cavalry forward to crush their centre. Hemu was on the cusp of victory when he was wounded in the eye by a Mughal arrow and collapsed unconscious. This triggered a panic in his army which broke formation and fled.

Aftermath
The elephant carrying the wounded Hemu was captured and led to the Mughal camp. Bairam Khan asked the 13-year-old Akbar to behead Hemu, but he refused to take the sword to a dying man. Akbar was persuaded to touch Hemu's head with his sword after which Bairam Khan executed him. Hemu's head was sent to Kabul while his body was gibbeted on a gate in Delhi. A minaret was subsequently constructed of the heads of the other dead.

Hemu's family who lived in Machari (near Alwar) was captured by Pir Muhammad. Pir Muhammad offered to spare the life of Hemu's elderly father if he converted to Islam. When the old man refused, he was executed. Hemu's Smadhi Sthal, constructed during Akbar's reign by supporters, supposedly on the spot where he died, is now occupied by migrant muslims and converted to a dargAh.

1b47927547.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°57′44.86″.
1b47927547.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°57′44.86″, 0°57′40.55″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 0°59′14.56″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 2°22′19.46″ W). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 1°56′59.42″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.24, elongation 2°54′24.65″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1b78277018.b: Observed on Mr̥gaśīrṣam nakshatra of Makaraḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
1b78277018.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Nagan, a skilled king of hunters from Uduppur in Pottapi Nadu, was a devout follower of Bhagavan Subramanya. He and his wife, Tattai, were blessed with a child named Tinnanar, who was believed to be the reincarnation of Arjuna. Tinnanar, raised as a hunter, excelled in archery and succeeded his father as the king at a young age. Despite his occupation, he practiced non-violence towards young ones, females, diseased animals, etc. and spiritually, he had already eliminated inner vices like lust, anger, greed, vanity, jealousy, etc.

One day, Tinnanar chased a pig that had escaped its net, leading to an intense pursuit that ended with Tinnanar killing the pig. Exhausted and thirsty, he and his companions sought water and rest. Tinnanar experienced a profound spiritual transformation as he climbed a nearby hill, losing his body consciousness and feeling an overwhelming love for Bhagavan Shiva. On the hill, he found a temple dedicated to Bhagavan Shiva and was moved to tears, feeling a deep connection with the deity.

Tinnanar's devotion led him to bring food to the temple daily, offering the best pieces of meat after tasting them himself. His actions disturbed his friends and family, who thought he had gone mad. One day, the temple's priest, Shivagochariar, was horrified to find the temple desecrated by Tinnanar's unconventional worship, which included water from his mouth for 'Abhishekam', and decoration of the Lingam with flowers worn on his head!

Despite Shivagochariar's efforts to purify the temple and conduct traditional worship, Tinnanar continued his practices, standing guard at the temple entrance after each of his rituals.

Shivagochariar prayed for intervention, and Bhagavan Shiva appeared in his dream and instructed him to witness Tinnanar's actions. On the sixth day, while at his usual quest to gather food for Bhagavan Shiva, Tinnanar encountered ominous signs. In his selfless devotion, Tinnanar was more concerned for the deity than for himself and these signs sparked a fear that something untoward had befallen Bhagavan!  Upon reaching the temple, he was devastated to find blood flowing from the deity's right eye. In his grief, he dropped all the worship items and tried to treat the deity's eye with herbs, but the bleeding persisted. Driven by a thought of equivalent sacrifice --- ‘flesh for flesh’ --- he removed his own right eye with an arrow and placed it on the deity, and the bleeding miraculously stopped. Overwhelmed with joy and dancing in ecstasy, he now noticed the deity's left eye bleeding. He was clear on how to stop this bleeding --- but how would he place the second eye having lost his vision? He planted his foot over the deity's left eye on the Lingam to guide himself! Just as he was about to extract his left eye, Bhagavan Shiva intervened, grasping his hand and affectionately addressing him as Kannappa (thrice), thus transforming Tinnanar into Kannappar. Bhagavan held him close, restoring his vision and granting him a divine status. Shivagochariar, the temple priest, witnessed this act of supreme devotion and understood its true nature.

The story also carries a deeper, symbolic meaning. Tinnanar's journey represents the spiritual conquest over inner evils, including ego (symbolized by the wild pig). Accompanied by representations of good and evil (Nanan and Kadan), Tinnanar's pursuit of the pig signifies the battle with one's own vices and the embrace of positive samskaras (impressions). The culmination of his journey, where he chooses to worship Bhagavan alone, symbolizes the ultimate renunciation of even good tendencies for pure, unadulterated devotion. Tinnanar's willingness to sacrifice his own eyes for the deity epitomizes complete self-surrender, the pinnacle of devotion that leads to divine revelation and realization.

𑌉𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌯𑌤𑍍 𑌕𑌿𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌅𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍇 𑌦𑍋𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌃---  
𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍈 𑌮𑍋𑌹𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌮𑌃।  
𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌭𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌕𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌘𑍋𑌰𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑌚𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑌃॥

𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌸𑍌𑌤𑌿𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑌿𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌦𑍇𑌶𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌿𑌂𑌶𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃---

𑌤𑌤𑍋 𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌋𑌤𑍂𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌷𑌟𑍍 𑌸𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍁𑌃।

𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌽𑌦𑌿𑌤𑌿𑌦𑍈𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌸𑍁।

𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍇 𑌜𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌥𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌨𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌕𑍌𑌸𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌜𑌨𑌯𑌦𑍍 𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌂 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌮𑍍॥௧-௧௮-௧௦॥

1ba685ccc1.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′23.62″.
1ba685ccc1.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′23.62″, 0°37′06.06″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′43.19″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′37.10″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′06.81″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°37′54.51″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1badf8ff40.d: Anadhyayana on account of aṣṭamī. Several tithis in a month are nitya-anadhyayana days, including prathamā, aṣṭamī, chaturdaśī, amāvāsyā and pūrṇimā. Manu has said that performing adhyayana on these days destroys the Guru (Amavasya), Shishya (Chaturdashi) and the vīrya of the brahma (vēda) itself (Ashtami/Purnima). Similarly, Jabali Rishi has said that Adhyayana on prathama hurts the buddhi while adhyayana on chaturdaśī hurts the brahma (vēda) itself!
1badf8ff40.s:
𑌹𑌾𑌰𑍀𑌤𑌃—  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍋𑌃।

1bb15e955f.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in ārdrā mithunam, center-to-center separation 0°51′42.70″.
1bb15e955f.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°51′42.70″, 0°51′19.75″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°03′50.64″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.94, elongation 35°43′04.28″ W). śukraḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°55′33.34″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.96, elongation 35°43′41.53″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1d0283a649.d: The fine autodidact pure math genius rAmAnujan was born by the grace of nAmagiri-amma to shrInivAsa ayyangAr. Under the devI's inspiration, he made substantial contributions to mathematical analysis, number theory, infinite series, and continued fractions, including solutions to mathematical problems then considered unsolvable. Ramanujan initially developed his own mathematical research in isolation. Finally he succeeded in getting GH Hardy's attention and patronage. He cried as they cut his shikhA. Used to recite sanskrit conjugations. Died at age 32. As late as 2011 and again in 2012, researchers continued to discover that mere comments in his writings about 'simple properties' and 'similar outputs' for certain findings were themselves profound and subtle number theory results that remained unsuspected until nearly a century after his death.

1d946e8151.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°36′15.29″.
1d946e8151.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°36′15.29″, 0°36′01.87″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°15′32.19″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.71, elongation 25°42′14.80″ W). śukraḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°39′16.91″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.87, elongation 25°39′40.36″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

1e2b3092fc.b: Observed on Kr̥ṣṇa-Aṣṭamī tithi of Jyaiṣṭhaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
1e2b3092fc.d:
The Wari (pilgrimage) is a centuries-old tradition in Maharashtra, India, involving a ceremonial procession of devotees (Warkaris) accompanying the Padukas (symbolic footprints) of saints to the Vithoba temple in Pandharpur. The two most prominent processions originate from the towns of Dehu and Alandi.

The procession of Sant Dnyaneshwar, affectionately known as Mauli (māūlī), begins one day later than the Dehu Yatra, from Āl̤andī on Jyeshtha Vadya Ashtami. This route is slightly shorter than the Dehu route but is equally arduous and spiritually significant. It often meets the Tukaram Pālkhī at specific junctures or converges near Pune before proceeding separately. Departing from the Samadhi Mandir, the Pālkhī moves to Pune, staying at the Pālkhī Vithoba Mandir in Bhavani Peth. The most visually dramatic leg of the journey follows as the devotees pull the heavy chariot up the steep Dive Ghat to reach Sāswaḍ, where the Pālkhī stays for two days. The route traverses the historic town of Jejuri—sacred to Lord Khandoba—and the village of Vālhe. Upon entering the Satara district, the procession halts at Loṇanda, famous for its unique sheep Ringan, and then Taraḍgaon. The journey continues through the princely town of Phalṭaṇ and onto Baraḍ. As it enters Solapur district, the halts include Nātepute, Māl̤shiras, and Vel̤āpūr, which hosts a spectacular Ringan. After a stop at Bhaṇḍīshegaon, the Mauli Pālkhī also arrives at Wākhari on Ashadhi Shuddha Dashami.

1e4a8d994f.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°57′44.97″.
1e4a8d994f.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°57′44.97″, 0°57′40.66″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 0°59′14.73″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 2°22′19.30″ W). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 1°56′59.70″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.24, elongation 2°54′24.51″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

Bhama Shah, a vaishya, was a great general, adviser, minister of Mewar, who was later promoted to post of Prime Minister of Mewar by Maharana Pratap, to whom he served as close aide and confidante. He along with his younger brother Tarachand fought in several battles for Mewar.

After Maharana Pratap was defeated by Akbar in the Battle of Haldighati, had no funds at all to carry on the fight, and his family was close to starvation. At this point, Bhama shah and his brother Tarachand, presented their wealth to maharana Pratap, who was overwhelmed.

1f11b3f6e4.d: While this is traditionally celebrated in Dhanurmasa, given the precession of equinoxes, it would be ideal to celebrate it in the corresponding tropical solar month, given that is the start of the uṣahkāla for the Devatas. A very early morning puja is performed, typically with mudgānnam as naivedyam. Begets fruit equivalent to performing puja for a thousand years! The two ayana-s of the Sun are night and day for the Devas. 30 of these days become a month. The uṣahkāla of their day starts in chāpamāsa i.e. dhanurmāsa (although the shloka refers to the sidereal month, it appears logical to use the tropical month, owing to its association with uttarāyaṇam). Therefore, one must strive to perform uṣahkāla-pujā in this month, before sunrise --- a ṣōḍaśōpachāra-pūjā. Following this, one must perform Sandhyavandam and upasthanam! The Shivapurana also extols the uniqueness of the early morning puja in this month, suggesting that one must perform rudrābhiṣeka.
1f11b3f6e4.s:

1f4851cd97.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śukraḥ in āśrēṣā karkaṭaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°30′35.64″.
1f4851cd97.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°30′35.64″, 0°30′28.32″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at āśrēṣā-3 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°44′29.07″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -2.04, elongation 1°45′14.43″ W). śukraḥ at āśrēṣā-3 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°13′53.44″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 1°14′56.58″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
1f4851cd97.s:
𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌗𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍂𑌰𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇  
  
𑌷𑌣𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌭𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌭𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑍇 𑌯𑍌𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌭𑌮𑍍।  
--𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 (𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣)

1f5f9df093.s:
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑍇 𑌶𑌿𑌵𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌯𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌶𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌿॥  
𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑍋 𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰।  
𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍇𑌶 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌪𑌯𑌾 𑌹𑌰॥  
𑌮𑌦𑌨𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌨-𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌵𑌚𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿---  
𑌯𑌦𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾।  
𑌆𑌰𑌬𑍍𑌧𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌫𑌲𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌯𑍇॥  
  
𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍂 𑌰𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌕𑍋𑌽𑌸𑌿  
𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍀 𑌆𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑍌  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌕𑌣𑍍𑌠𑍋𑌽𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍॥  
𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌹𑌲𑌂 𑌹𑌰 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌂  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸𑌪𑌦𑌿 𑌯𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌨𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍।  
𑌦𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌶𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌧𑌿 𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇  
𑌸 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑌶𑍁𑌪𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍁𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾 𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌾 𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌾 𑌶𑌿𑌵 𑌪𑌾𑌵𑌨𑍀𑌤𑌿  
𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌰 𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌿 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌕𑍂𑌟𑌃।  
𑌸𑌂𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑌾𑌯 𑌜𑌗𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌤𑍍  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌦𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾 𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍇𑌶𑌾𑌨 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌭𑌗𑍀𑌰𑌥𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌂 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌭𑍇𑌦𑌹𑍇𑌤𑌵𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌---  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍁𑌭𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌸𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌨𑍈𑌕𑌦𑍇𑌶𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑍇𑌽𑌧𑌿𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍂𑌨𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌪𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌦𑌿𑌨 𑌏𑌵  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌨𑍀𑌯𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍍।

1f6f116869.d:
Captain Vikram Batra of 13th battalion, Jammu and Kashmir Rifles, called Shershah by pAkistani jihAdist enemies for his prior bravery, died capturing Point 4875 on this day.

Area Flat Top, an adjacent peak and part of enemy defences on Point 4875 was being held by Capt. N.A. Nagappa till he was rendered unconscious by a shell. Vikram Batra, though still recovering from earlier injuries, insisted on going up to help. Seeing Batra's determination to save Peak 4875 and the honour of his battalion, several of his company's soldiers volunteered to accompany him even before any official orders had been issued. Just before leaving, Batra along with the 25 men of D Coy who were to accompany him, prayed at the Durga Mata temple. 

His company was tasked to clear a narrow feature with sharp cuttings on either side and heavily fortified enemy defences that covered the only approach to it. For speedy operation, Captain Batra assaulted the enemy position along a narrow ridge and engaged the enemy in a fierce hand –to-hand fight and killed five enemy soldiers at point blank range. Despite sustaining grave injuries, he crawled towards the enemy and hurled grenades clearing the position. Though it was pitch dark, on a foggy snowy night with a near vertical climb, Batra downed 3 machine gun positions. By the time they reached the top, it was daylight. Not finding an alternate route to reach Capt Nagappa, they decided to make a direct daylight frontal assault. Under heavy fire from enemy machine guns and grenade launchers, the captain shouted 'Durga mata ki jai', and charged the sangar firing incessantly from his AK-47. Despite injury, he managed to breach it, punch a pAki soldier on the nose before bayoneting him (and downing another). They further captured a machine gun nest, killing 4 pAkis. Realising that one of his men was shot, Batra decided to evacuate him - positioning himself in the front saying 'You have a family and children to go back to, I'm not even married.'. Then he was fatally shot by enemy sniper, and an RPG splinter caught him.

Earlier victory: During ‘Operation Vijay’, on 20 June 1999, Captain Vikram Batra, Commander Delta Company was tasked to attack Point 5140 of Dras. Leading from the front, he in a daredevil assault, pounced on the enemy and killed four of them in a hand-to hand fight.  He radioed the predetermined code: 'Yeh Dil Mange More!'. Batra was promoted to the rank of captain, and congradulated by the Army chief.

1f890182a0.d:
On this day, Awrangzeb reimposed the discriminatory Jazia tax on Hindus.

This was just a month after the death of the powerful rAjaputra Jasvant singh rAthoD, and the fanatic had been waiting for the opportunity.

Translated order
As all the arms of the religious Emperor (Aurangzeb) were directed to the spreading of the law of Islam and the overthrow of the practices of the infidels he issued orders to the high diwani officers that from 1st Rabi ul awwal, in obedience to the Quranic injuction 'till they pay commutation money (jazia) with the hand in humility' and in agreement with the canonical traditions, jazia should be collected from the infidels of the capital and the provinces.

1f9303842a.b: Observed on Śukla-Prathamā tithi of Vaiśākhaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
1f9303842a.d: Vaiśākha-māsaḥ begins today --- special for various dānam's such as buttermilk, pānakam etc. Brings unlimited puṇyam! In the Mahābhārata, it is said that one who, with controlled senses (jitendriyaḥ), observes the month of Vaiśākha with ekabhakta discipline (one meal a day), and bathes early in the morning — whether man or woman — attains excellence among their community. In the Vāmana Purāṇa, it is stated that during Vaiśākha, one should offer fragrant garlands and perfumes to distinguished brāhmaṇas to please Madhusūdana (Viṣṇu).
1f9303842a.s:
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௪௧॥  
𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌧𑌨𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌭𑍂𑌮𑍌 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑌃।  
𑌨 𑌤𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌦𑍃𑌶𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌘𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥௪௨॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌯𑍇।  
𑌜𑌮𑍍𑌬𑍀𑌰𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌸𑍋𑌪𑍇𑌤𑌂 𑌲𑌸𑌲𑍍𑌲𑌵𑌣𑌮𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍॥௪௩॥  
𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌰𑍁𑌚𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌮𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌮𑌵𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍।  
𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌧𑌿𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌘𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌯𑍇॥௪௪॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌹𑌂 𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌮𑌿 𑌭𑍂𑌮𑌿𑌪।  
𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍁𑌲𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨𑌵𑌲𑍍𑌲𑌭𑍇॥௪௫॥  
𑌸 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌯𑍋 𑌘𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑍇𑌜𑌸𑍋 𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌂 𑌗𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌯𑍇॥  
𑌸𑍋𑌽𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌮𑍋𑌦𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍇॥௪௬॥  
𑌉𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍁𑌗𑍁𑌡𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌗𑍇 𑌰𑌵𑍌।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌪𑍇 𑌵𑌸𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌧𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌮𑍍॥௪௭॥  
𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍇𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍁𑌦𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌂 𑌸𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌨𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾 𑌤𑌾𑌪𑍋𑌪𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌯𑍇।  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌾𑌯 𑌚 𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌕𑌮𑍍॥௪௮॥  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌕𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌨𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌯𑍇।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍋𑌃 𑌸𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍॥௪௯॥  
𑌸𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌕𑌂 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍇 𑌸𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌯𑍇।  
𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑍁𑌧𑌾𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌨 𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑌃॥௫௦॥  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌕𑌂 𑌚𑍂𑌤𑌸𑍁𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌵𑌫𑌲𑌸𑌂𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌣𑌿 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌨𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍॥௫௧॥  
—𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌅𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍇  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇---  
𑌨𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌰𑍇𑌦𑍇𑌕𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌯𑍋 𑌜𑌿𑌤𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌃।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌯𑍀 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀 𑌵𑌾 𑌜𑌾𑌤𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌜𑍇𑌤𑍍॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌵𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌚 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌭𑍀𑌣𑌿 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍇𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌮𑍁𑌖𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑍇॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।

1feb289a4a.d: On this day, Pandit Birbal Dhar entered with Sikh soldiers into Kashmir as a victor over afghAns. He had made a daring and costly escape (loosing wife, daughter in law) from Azam Khan's court to raNajIt singh at lahore via gulAb singh in jammu.

1febfba75c.b: Observed on Paurṇamāsī tithi of Āṣāḍhaḥ (lunar) month (Prāktanāruṇōdayaḥ/paraviddha).
1febfba75c.d: Perform snana four ghatikas before sunrise (during aruṇodayaḥ, when the Moon is still up, on the full-moon days of āṣāḍha, kārttika, māgha and vaiśākha – hence the name ā-kā-mā-vai) bestows strength, beauty, fame, dharma, knowledge, happiness, fortitude and health.
1febfba75c.s:
𑌉𑌦𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌕𑍍 𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌨𑌾𑌡𑌿𑌕𑌾 𑌅𑌰𑍁𑌣𑍋𑌦𑌯𑌃।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌂𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌸 𑌹𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌃॥  
𑌬𑌲𑌂 𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌂 𑌯𑌶𑍋 𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌂 𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌸𑍁𑌖𑌂 𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍍।  
𑌆𑌰𑍋𑌗𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌕𑍍 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃॥  
𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍀 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍀 𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌷𑌾𑌢𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌾𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌿𑌹𑍀𑌨𑌾 𑌵𑍈 𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌰𑍌𑌰𑌵𑌗𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌨𑌃॥
